segments.say: Lesson 5. Embeddings & Similarity. Meaning as coordinates: how vectors power semantic search, and cosine versus dot versus euclidean.

An embedding turns a piece of text into a list of numbers (a vector) so that texts with similar meaning get similar numbers. That lets computers search by meaning, not exact words. Here is an analogy. A library shelved by topic instead of title: books about dogs sit near books about puppies. To find related books you just look nearby.

Why does this matter? The core of semantic search and rag retrieval. Also used for clustering, dedup, recommendations and semantic caching. A few key words. Vector: An ordered list of numbers, for example 1,536 of them. Embedding model: A model that maps text to vectors. Cosine similarity: How closely two vectors point the same way ( minus 1 to 1). Semantic search: Finding results by meaning.
Meaning becomes geometry. An embedding model turns text into a vector, a list of for example 768–3072 numbers. Here we squash it to 2D so you can see it.
Texts with similar meaning land close together. "dog" and "cat" share an animals neighbourhood.
. while "car" and "truck" sit far away in a vehicles region. Distance equals semantic difference.
A new query, "puppy", gets embedded too. The nearest stored vector is "dog" (cosine 0.91). That lookup is semantic search.
Directions carry meaning: king minus man plus woman about queen. The same "+female" offset appears in both pairs.
In rag you embed every chunk once, store the vectors, then embed each question and fetch its nearest neighbours.

segments.say: Many embedding models output unit-length vectors. Then cosine equals the dot product, which is cheaper, so vector D Bs often just use the dot product.

What an embedding is. A dense vector that captures meaning. Models like OpenAI text-embedding-3, Cohere Embed, B G E, E5 or Sentence-Transformers are trained so that texts with similar meaning get similar vectors.

Where you use them. Semantic search / rag retrieval: nearest neighbours to the query vector. Clustering & dedup: group similar tickets and logs. Classification: train a cheap classifier on embeddings. Semantic cache: reuse an answer if a new question is close enough to an old one. Recommendations / anomaly detection.

Choosing an embedding model. Dimensions: more dims can capture more nuance but cost more storage and search time. Some models (Matryoshka) let you truncate dimensions. Domain fit: check retrieval benchmarks (for example the M T E B leaderboard), then test on your data. Max input tokens: limits chunk size. Golden rule: query and documents must use the same model. If you change the model you must re-embed everything.
Analogy. A giant library where books are shelved by meaning, not title. To find answers you walk to where your question would be shelved and grab the nearby books.

Common mistakes. Mixing embedding models between indexing and querying. Expecting embeddings to match exact I Ds or error codes. Dense vectors blur exact tokens, so use hybrid search with B M 25. Embedding chunks that are too long, which averages away the meaning.

Say it in the interview. "Embeddings map text to vectors where semantic similarity becomes geometric closeness, usually measured with cosine. In rag I embed chunks offline into a vector index, embed the query at runtime and do approximate nearest-neighbour search. Because dense retrieval misses exact keywords like error codes, I pair it with B M 25 in a hybrid setup.".

Similarity metrics. Cosine: angle between vectors, -1 to 1, default for text; ignores length. Dot product: sum of products, unbounded, vectors already normalized (then equals cosine), fastest. Euclidean (L2): straight-line distance, 0 to ∞, some image / older models; magnitude matters.

Sparse versus dense. Captures: exact keywords, meaning / synonyms. "reset pwd" "change password": miss, match. Error code "E-4012": exact hit, often fuzzy. Cost: cheap, no G P U, needs embedding model.

A likely interview question: Explain embeddings to a non-technical manager. A strong answer: They turn text into coordinates so that things that mean the same thing end up close together. Search then becomes "find the nearest points".
That's it for Embeddings & Similarity. Now play the quiz and games in the app to lock it in. See you in the next lesson.
